Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) employ traditional spatial convolutions that weight each pixel location across a kernel's bounds equally. This uniform treatment of locations may hinder the effective learning of edge-sensitive features, prompting the exploration of dynamic, location-aware approaches such as Dynamic Filters (DFs) and Split Kernels (SKs). A major drawback of these methods is the significant computational and memory resources required for multiple kernel learnable weights per layer. In contrast, we propose utilizing Global Mean Pooling (GMP) layers, typically employed in depthwise convolutions, as effective dynamic feature adaptors and present two variants: a GMP-based dynamic starting point for feature mapping along an edge of an image and another for freely specifying a starting point within the image. Our GMP-based solutions require essentially zero additional parameters and demonstrate equivalent or improved performance compared to traditional CNNs and existing dynamic architectures on multiple benchmarks. Our findings provide a novel perspective on the effectiveness of GMP in leveraging pixel location information and offer a low-resource alternative to traditional CNNs that may attract industry interest. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions. One such mission concept, involving the use of MuLE optics and a single large Format Image Depletion Multi-Application CMOS (MAMP) sensor, was evaluated through a systematic analysis of its performance. The results showed that a MuLE-optics system combined with a MAMP sensor would be capable of detecting transients with a signal-to-noise ratio of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1 within an field of view of ~1.5x10^-4 steradians. This performance meets the requirements for future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions and could be a highly effective imaging strategy for upcoming wide-field X-ray sky monitors. Such monitors would be ideal for detecting impulsive X-ray events such as gas giant pulsars, studying the spectrum of blazars, and conducting transient event search for evidence of dark matter. The proposed MuLE optics arrangement also offers significant technical advantages over traditional LE optics, including a much reduced risk of contamination, easier mass production, and a simpler system for determining the focal point of X-rays. The MuLE optics design is highly effective and could be employed in various wide-field X-ray imaging applications, ranging from sky monitors to instruments for analyzing the spectrum of targets. The same design could also be used in visible light monitors for detecting transients, such as supernovae, and analyzing the spectrum of celestial objects. The technical details of the MuLE optics design could be easily adapted for use in visible light imaging instruments that employ microstructured arrays of lenses, such as LE optics, at the entrance of the instrument. This would allow such instruments to greatly decrease the number of image sensors required and increase the sensitivity to low-level signals by further improving the overall quantum efficiency of the instrument. This report details our methods that led to 1st and 2nd place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on identifying skin carcinomas using images and outlier data. A combination of convolutional neural networks (CNN) and outlier analysis was used to classify images into healthy, benign, and malignant categories. In this study, we address the inverse problem of determining the properties of a porous acoustic material whose structure is linked to that of an accompanying structural material, when both are impacted and vibrate in harmony with each other. A numerical example is provided where the approach is tested and verified by calculating the porous material's properties through its interaction with a circular steel plate. When a steel stick is placed on the plate, causing it to vibrate in a way that transfers sound to the porous material, the resulting properties are found to be highly accurate, proving the effectiveness of this new approach. In addition to determining the material's properties, the research also explores the possibility of creating a map of the internal structure of the material based on its vibration patterns, which could be highly beneficial for non-invasive diagnostic techniques. Furthermore, the authors propose using phase contrast imaging as a possible method for visualizing these maps. The techniques developed in this study can be applied to various porous materials with similar structures, and their potential uses extend beyond acoustic performance, including applications in thermal insulation and vibration reduction. The researchers also emphasize the importance of further investigation into optimizing these materials' performance by modifying their internal structures. The paper's findings have been published in the AIAA Journal of Aircraft and Spacecraft Systems in January 2023, under the title "A Boundary Integral-Finite Element Method for Structural-Acoustic Coupling in Porous Materials" and the accompanying material properties were analyzed using the software Comsol Multiphysics 5.6.

Within the context of a specific minimalistic field theory, we have identified the simplest possible implementation of the seesaw mechanism, wherein a weak-scale WIMP rises above the invisibility threshold for colliding particles, all while guaranteeing the stability of the vacuum state. This stability is ensured through the production of light heavy Majorons, which decay slowly, making way for a long-lived heavy Majoron, capable of decaying into pairs of neutrinos. A two-component dark matter model emerges, with one component aligning with the minimal paradigm for spontaneous symmetry breaking, while the other component alignates with the nearly massless heavy neutrino. Through a detailed analysis of spectrum constraints derived from LHC and astrophysical data, we determine the possible parameters of this model, which includes the dark matter mass range ($0.1 \times 10^{3}$ eV to $10^{3}$ eV), heavy neutrino mass range ($10^{-3} \times 10^{3}$ eV to $10^{3}$ eV), heavy Majoron mass range ($10^{-3} \times 10^{3}$ eV to $10^{3}$ eV), heavy scalar mass range ($0.1 \times 10^{3}$ eV to $10^{3}$ eV), mixing angle range ($10^{-9} \times 10^{-3}$ to $10^{-3}$), and quartic coupling range ($10^{-14} \times 10^{-10}$ to $10^{-10}$). Furthermore, we calculate the possible values for relic density, direct detection cross-section, heavy Majoron decay constant, heavy scalar decay constant, heavy neutrino mixing angle, heavy neutrino mass splitting, light heavy Majoron lifetime, heavy scalar lifetime, and effective neutrino mass at low energy experiments. Lastly, we believe that this easiest possible implementation of the seesaw mechanism for a WIMP dark matter model, alongside the vacuum stability guarantee, offers a compelling framework that could potentially explain various astrophysical phenomena, including the abundance of dark matter, the disappearance of neutrinos, and the near masslessness of heavy neutrinos, all while providing multiple possibilities for future low-energy experiments.
